bio.en: Ayo Omojola is Chief Product Officer at Carbon Health and previously the founding product lead on Cash App's banking team at Square, where he co-created the Cash Card and scaled it into a nine-figure revenue line.
bio.zh: Ayo Omojola 是 Carbon Health 首席产品官，此前是 Square 旗下 Cash App 银行团队的创始产品负责人，共同打造了 Cash Card 并将其发展为上亿美元收入线。

summary.en: Ayo shares hard-won lessons from building and scaling the Cash Card and Cash App, emphasizing the importance of differentiation when building any consumer product. He argues for going “unreasonably deep” to understand constraints—especially in regulated industries—and that problem selection matters as much as problem solving. The conversation covers why small teams beat big ones, the benefits of hiring founders, and first-principles thinking for product and team building.
summary.zh: Ayo 分享了构建和扩展 Cash Card 与 Cash App 的宝贵经验，强调打造任何消费产品时“差异化”的重要性。他主张“极其深入”地理解约束（尤其在受监管行业），并认为“选对问题”与“解决问题”同样重要。对话涵盖为何小团队优于大团队、雇佣创始人的好处，以及产品与团队建设中的第一性原理思维。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: Cash App, as a team we really cared about what we could do that was different and better than what else existed in-market. Being different is not enough, because it's very easy to build a thing that's different from what exists today, because you just have to look at what exists today and build something else. Being better is not enough, because it's also easy to say, "Hey, I'm going to make this thing better, and just charge you more money for it." It has to be better than what exists today in a way that matters to the end user, and for us for a long time it was when someone says, "Hey, why are you betting on Venmo?" I'd be like, "Try and send me a dollar that I can use now," and there was only one app you could do it with.
turns.zh: Cash App，作为一个团队，我们真正关心我们能做些什么，与市场上现有的其他产品不同且更好。与众不同是不够的，因为构建一个与当今存在的东西不同的东西非常容易，因为你只需要看看今天存在的东西并构建其他东西。做得更好是不够的，因为也很容易说：“嘿，我要把这件事做得更好，然后向你收取更多的钱。”它必须以对最终用户重要的方式比当今存在的更好，对我们来说很长一段时间，当有人说，“嘿，你为什么押注于 Venmo？”我会说，“试着给我寄一美元，我现在可以使用”，但只有一个应用程序可以做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: In 2015 I'd been at Cash App for about a year, had massive burnout from the last company, went through IC, kind of like did a hard pivot, imploded a little bit, stuff kind of picked up, sold the company eventually. And my brother, who's my co-founder, and I had this idea, and I think it was actually from printing and mailing my section 83B for something that I'd done. And I was like, "Why can't I just go onto the internet and do this?" And so I had this idea to build an application where you could give it a document and an address, and we would print it and mail it for you. And it was right around when Lob was founded, which was... (05:13): Lob is like this printing and mailing API. So we built this thing called Mailform, I think it's like one of the top consumer print and mail things on the internet. I'm sure many people who listen to this will have used it for... And then we had to figure out how to grow it, and the way that I actually learned how to do SEO was running around the internet, trying to find ways to tell people that we did this, and that they would find us. And we actually ended up, funny as it turns out, we ended up building a whole sort of SEO content infrastructure around it that has really impacted my thinking. But all the answers on Quora were me just trying to get people... You know, if you remember like 2014, Quora was like this massive thing. (06:00): So all the answers on Quora were me trying to get people who might be thinking about the problem that we were solving to realize that we exist.
turns.zh: 2015 年，我在 Cash App 工作了大约一年，对上一家公司感到严重倦怠，经历了 IC，有点像做了一次硬转型，有点内爆，东西有所回升，最终卖掉了公司。我的兄弟，我的联合创始人，我有这个想法，我认为这实际上是因为我所做的事情打印和邮寄了我的 83B 部分。我当时想，“为什么我不能上网做这件事呢？”因此，我产生了构建一个应用程序的想法，您可以在其中为其提供文档和地址，然后我们将打印并邮寄给您。就在 Lob 成立的时候，当时... (05:13)：Lob 就像这个打印和邮寄 API。所以我们建立了这个叫做 Mailform 的东西，我认为它就像互联网上顶级的消费者打印和邮件产品之一。我相信很多听过这个的人都会用它来……然后我们必须弄清楚如何发展它，而我实际上学习如何进行 SEO 的方式是在互联网上运行，试图找到方法告诉人们我们做到了这一点，并且他们会找到我们。事实上，有趣的是，我们最终围绕它构建了一整套 SEO 内容基础设施，这确实影响了我的想法。但 Quora 上的所有答案都是我试图让人们知道的……你知道，如果你还记得 2014 年，Quora 就是一个巨大的东西。 (06:00)：所以 Quora 上的所有答案都是我试图让那些可能正在思考我们正在解决的问题的人意识到我们的存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Let's talk about your Cash App experience, which I imagine was a pretty transformative period in your career. And from my understanding it had a major impact on the success of the app and the business that was built there. To give folks a bit of scale and understanding of just the Cash App in general, can you just briefly talk about how big was it when you joined, like the scale of the app, and then whatever you can share about just the scale today.
turns.zh: 惊人的。让我们谈谈您的 Cash App 体验，我认为这是您职业生涯中一个相当变革的时期。据我了解，它对应用程序和在那里建立的业务的成功产生了重大影响。为了让人们对现金应用程序有一定的规模和了解，您能否简要谈谈您加入时它的规模有多大，例如应用程序的规模，然后您今天可以分享有关规模的任何信息。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: When I joined Cash App was probably sub 50K actives, like people moving money. Today I think it's north of 50 million actives on a monthly basis, will all different types of money movement, like Bitcoin, PP, card, stocks. And I think it's something like north of 70 or 80 million actives on an annual basis.
turns.zh: 当我加入 Cash App 时，活跃人数可能低于 5 万，比如人们转移资金。今天，我认为每月的活跃人数超过 5000 万，所有不同类型的资金流动，如比特币、PP、卡、股票。我认为每年大约有 70 或 8000 万活跃用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, okay, great. What I want to talk a bit about is that Cash App to me is a rare example of a huge consumer app success story, I've been angel investing for a while now and I've just learned how rare consumer apps work. Like, they never work, and this one worked. Even within a big company, you think that there's a huge chance of something working if they have the support of a big company, and the platform, things like that. Still, they almost all fail. And so what I'm curious about is, what do you think you all did most right, one to launch it successfully in the consumer space, and then two, to keep it growing and scaling to where it got today?
turns.zh: 哇，好吧，太棒了。我想谈谈的是，Cash App 对我来说是一个巨大的消费者应用程序成功故事的罕见例子，我已经进行天使投资有一段时间了，我刚刚了解了罕见的消费者应用程序是如何工作的。就像，它们从来没有起作用，而这个起作用了。即使在一家大公司内，你也会认为，如果他们得到大公司和平台等的支持，那么事情就有很大的机会发挥作用。尽管如此，他们几乎都失败了。所以我很好奇的是，你们认为你们做得最正确的是什么，一是在消费者领域成功推出它，二是保持它的增长并扩展到今天的水平？

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: My perspective is that, and I think this is a, people don't like this kind of answer.
turns.zh: 我的观点是，我认为这是一个，人们不喜欢这种答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm exciting to hear this.
turns.zh: 听到这个我很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: But the thing Cash App did right was like 10 things, not one. There were like 10 things that actually best in class, like insane talent density, insane focus, very strong at fraud, a lot of the way Brian, and Dustin, and Jesse, and Dangi tried to organize the amount... Like you know, with Jack's support was just really firewalled from the rest of the square, the hero customer was the consumer, not the merchants, so it was like literally in 100% of the trade offs the consumer's needs came first. And that's a very, very hard thing to do, instead of accommodating like... It made people angry, actually. Really insane focus on design, incredible depth in... This is the thing that I think you will appreciate, but it's very hard to appreciate just as a consumer of things, people would be like, "Hey, what's the difference between you and Venmo?" (09:26): And the only reason you would ask that is if you just hadn't thought about it for a second. Now, today there's like a lot of convergence on features like... So Venmo's sort of caught up on a lot of the things. But at the time, Venmo didn't have push to debit, Venmo didn't have an instant. For like three or four years in the United States, the fastest and lowest-cost way to move money in the country between any two people who had bank accounts was Cash App. And I think that kind of changed in 2017, when PayPal, Venmo, Apple Cash, et cetera, kind of came out and launched all their things. And so I think actually it's possible that having done only one of those things well, Cash App might have been successful. But I think the reason it's differentially successful in the market today is the compound effect of all those things.
turns.zh: 但 Cash App 做对的事情大约有 10 件事，而不是一件。有大约 10 件事情实际上是同类中最好的，比如疯狂的人才密度、疯狂的专注、非常擅长欺诈，布莱恩、达斯汀、杰西和丹吉试图组织金额的很多方式……如你所知，杰克的支持与其他人真正隔离开来，英雄客户是消费者，而不是商家，所以就像字面意义上的，在 100% 的权衡中，消费者的需求是第一位的。这是一件非常非常困难的事情，而不是像……那样包容，实际上这让人们生气。对设计的疯狂关注，令人难以置信的深度......这是我认为你会欣赏的东西，但作为事物的消费者很难欣赏，人们会说，“嘿，你和 Venmo 之间有什么区别？” (09:26)：你问这个问题的唯一原因是你根本就没有考虑过这个问题。现在，今天的功能有很多融合，比如……所以 Venmo 在很多方面都赶上了。但当时，Venmo 没有推送借记功能，Venmo 没有即时功能。在美国大约三四年的时间里，在该国任何两个拥有银行账户的人之间转移资金的最快、成本最低的方式就是 Cash App。我认为这种情况在 2017 年发生了变化，当时 PayPal、Venmo、Apple Cash 等出现并推出了他们所有的产品。所以我认为实际上只要做好其中一件事，Cash App 就有可能取得成功。但我认为它在当今市场上取得不同成功的原因是所有这些因素的复合效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny

Is there stuff you extract from them, like, "Here's something that I'm going to do any time I'm building a consumer app"? turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: This is the thing I struggle with, I saw on Twitter somebody say this comment, that a lot of times when people describe their success to you what they're really saying is like, "This is my lottery ticket number." So to be honest, before I go down this diatribe I don't actually know which of the things are replicable. I just know kind of what I believe to be true, and I'm trying... Some of it worked, some of it not, et cetera. So I think Cash App, as a team we really cared about what we could do that was different and better than what else existed in market. And for us, for a long time it was instant, and if you look at all the products you'll see this sort of theme, of when you cash out there's an instant option. (11:20): When you get a cash card, we issue your card to you instantly. When you sell stocks, money's available instantly. When you sell Bitcoin, money's available instantly. Like literally, there's no like, "Oh, circle, circle, circle processing," it's like, "Available to spend." And I think there's something actually lasting about the concept of instant, because there still in the world today are like lots of businesses and processes that are like asynchronous, but not for any reason other than, that's just the way the world is. So I think that's like one thing that's kind of narrow. And then I would say another thing that I think is really broad is just being really crisp about why what you're doing is different and better than what exists today. And it's like, being different is not enough, because it's very easy to build a thing that's different form what exists today, because you just have to look at what exists today and build something else. (12:08): And being better is not enough, because it's also easy to say, "Hey, I'm going to make this thing better and just charge you more money for it." And so I think there's like, different... You optimize for doing a thing that's different, it has to be better than what exists today, and it has to be better than what exists today in a way that matters to the end user, or to the buyer, depending on what your market is. And then after all that, it also... You have to be in a domain that matters, because it's very easy to get those three right, to build like a really... How do I say this? A thing that's different and better than what exists today, in a way that matters to end users could also just be art. Which is just like, art is a complex thing to scale. (12:58): And so you have to like, then also get the economics right, get the entire pipeline of like how you ship, how you build, how you talk about it, all that stuff has to work as well.
turns.zh: 这是我一直在纠结的事情，我在推特上看到有人这样评论，很多时候，当人们向你描述他们的成功时，他们真正说的是，“这是我的彩票号码。”所以说实话，在我进行这种谩骂之前，我实际上并不知道哪些事情是可以复制的。我只知道我相信什么是真实的，并且我正在尝试......有些有效，有些无效，等等。所以我认为 Cash App，作为一个团队，我们真正关心的是我们能做些什么，与市场上现有的其他产品不同且更好。对于我们来说，很长一段时间它都是即时的，如果你查看所有产品，你会看到这种主题，即当你兑现时有一个即时选项。 (11:20)：当您拿到现金卡后，我们会立即向您发放卡。当您出售股票时，资金立即可用。当您出售比特币时，资金立即可用。就像字面意思一样，没有像“哦，循环，循环，循环处理”之类的，而是“可以花费”。我认为即时的概念实际上是持久的，因为当今世界仍然有很多类似异步的业务和流程，但没有任何原因，除了世界就是这样。所以我认为这就像是一件有点狭隘的事情。然后我想说另一件我认为非常广泛的事情就是非常明确地说明为什么你正在做的事情与今天的事情不同并且更好。就像，与众不同是不够的，因为构建一个与当今存在的东西不同的东西是很容易的，因为你只需要看看今天存在的东西并构建其他东西。 (12:08)：做得更好还不够，因为也很容易说，“嘿，我要把这件事做得更好，然后向你收取更多的钱。”所以我认为有一些不同......你优化做一件不同的事情，它必须比今天现有的更好，并且它必须以对最终用户或买家重要的方式比今天现有的更好，这取决于你的市场是什么。毕竟，它也......你必须处于一个重要的领域，因为很容易得到这三个权利，建立像一个真正......我怎么说呢？与当今存在的东西不同、更好、对最终用户而言重要的东西也可能只是艺术。就像艺术是一件复杂的事情一样。 (12:58)：所以你必须喜欢，然后还要获得正确的经济效益，获得整个管道，比如如何运输、如何建造、如何谈论它，所有这些东西也必须发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's some really great lessons there, just to kind of mirror back what you're saying. Just differentiation in this case ends up being really important, and if you're trying to disrupt someone doing something, like say Venmo. Like, you can't just be a better Venmo, you have to be different. And it sounds like instant was the differentiator in this case.
turns.zh: 我认为那里有一些非常好的教训，只是为了反映你所说的内容。在这种情况下，差异化最终变得非常重要，如果你想扰乱某人做某事，就像 Venmo 所说的那样。就像，你不能只是成为一个更好的 Venmo，你必须与众不同。在这种情况下，听起来即时是差异化因素。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: For a long time, yeah, yeah. Or rather, it was the cut through the clutter differentiator. There were actually like a lot of other sort of long tail of things that we were doing those different, but it was like, instant was the thing where when someone says, "Hey, why are you betting on Venmo?" I'd be like, "Try and send me a dollar that I can use now," and there was only one app you could do it with.
turns.zh: 好久了，是啊是啊。或者更确切地说，这是一种突破杂乱的差异化因素。实际上，我们做了很多不同的长尾事情，但就像，当有人说“嘿，你为什么押注于 Venmo？”时，就是即时的事情？我会说，“试着给我寄一美元，我现在可以使用”，但只有一个应用程序可以做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think the other element of this, it connects to something I'm working on in the newsletter, is when you're trying to find a big idea, especially in B2B, but in this case it worked in B2C, is just, it needs to be important, it needs to matter, like it can't be a better thing that nobody values highly, because then you will make money in B2B, and in B2C people won't even use it. So, these are really great. You mentioned in passing when we were preparing for this that Block was trying to kill the Cash App for a lot of time, early time.
turns.zh: 我认为这与我在时事通讯中所做的事情有关，就是当你试图找到一个伟大的想法时，尤其是在 B2B 领域，但在这种情况下，它在 B2C 中起作用，只是，它需要重要，它需要重要，就像它不可能是一个没有人高度重视的更好的事情，因为这样你就会在 B2B 中赚钱，而在 B2C 中人们甚至不会使用它。所以，这些真的很棒。你顺便提到，当我们为此做准备时，Block 很早就试图杀死 Cash App。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: I wouldn't say like Block was trying to kill the Cash App. I think that there were many, many people who worked there that absolutely... And I mean this in the nicest way, identities were tied with Square being a merchant business, believed that the investment in Cash App could have been better deployed elsewhere, didn't want to work on consumer. There was just like a myriad of... And then look, I'm sure people who were there [inaudible 00:14:44], like we probably also made mistakes, and didn't communicate well, and didn't sell it well, and so on. But there was a crazy amount of friction, I'll put it that way. A thing I will 100% give Brian credit for is, he was really effective at making sure that we had a shot.
turns.zh: 我不会说 Block 试图杀死 Cash App。我认为有很多很多人在那里工作，绝对......我的意思是，以最好的方式，身份与 Square 作为商业企业联系在一起，相信对 Cash App 的投资可以更好地部署在其他地方，不想为消费者工作。就像有无数...然后你看，我确信在场的人 [听不清 00:14:44]，就像我们可能也犯了错误，没有很好地沟通，也没有很好地销售，等等。但我会这么说，其中存在着巨大的摩擦。我百分百相信布莱恩的一点是，他在确保我们有机会方面确实非常有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Zooming out for a moment and thinking about just Square and Block, and how they operate as a product company and as a business, is there anything that you've taken away from that experience that you bring with you to where you are now? Which, I want to talk about next.
turns.zh: 稍微缩小一下范围，想想 Square 和 Block，以及它们作为产品公司和企业的运作方式，您从现在的经历中学到了什么？接下来我想谈谈这一点。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: I don't know necessarily if this was intentional, my guess is it was probably just like a consequence of Square going through, going public and trying to be sort of a rigorous financial institution. I think when you are in a large organization, trying to do a actually new thing, I think small teams are better than big ones, period. And forcing the teams to be like super, sort of thoughtful about hitting milestones and actually adding value, because there's this thing people say about like, "Hey, the startup within a startup, everything's fake." And the reason I think it's fake is because when you're a startup you actually worry about paying the people who work for you, and when you aren't inside of a company you just don't. (16:02): And there is just a difference between having that existential fear of, "Are we going to be here tomorrow, and not?" So I think a consequence of not having that existential fear is that it's easy to just be like, "Hey, I need more resources," and the organization has some habits around how you acquire resources, and if the leadership of the... If the leadership building the new thing happened to be good at that, you can have growth in a new project's people size that doesn't match the new project's success and potential. And I think that actually ends up... It ends up being a tax over time.
turns.zh: 我不一定知道这是否是故意的，我的猜测是这可能就像 Square 经历、上市并试图成为一家严格的金融机构的结果一样。我认为当你在一个大型组织中尝试做一件真正的新事情时，我认为小团队比大团队更好，就这样。并迫使团队像超级一样，对达到里程碑并实际增加价值进行深思熟虑，因为人们会说，“嘿，初创公司中的初创公司，一切都是假的。”我之所以认为这是假的，是因为当你是一家初创公司时，你实际上担心为你工作的人付钱，而当你不在公司内部时，你就不会担心。 (16:02)：存在的恐惧与“我们明天会在这里吗？”之间是有区别的。因此，我认为，没有这种存在主义恐惧的后果是，很容易就会说，“嘿，我需要更多资源”，而且组织在如何获取资源方面有一些习惯，如果……如果构建新事物的领导层恰好擅长于此，那么新项目的人员规模增长可能与新项目的成功和潜力不匹配。我认为这实际上最终会......随着时间的推移，它最终会成为一种税收。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point, I didn't think about asking about that. But in this case it was a startup within a company that did well, and I also agree, it rarely works and it did here. What is it do you think that was so central to making it work? I know you just talked about it, how would you summarize just like, "Here's the thing everyone should do when they're maybe starting something small within a big company that's new"?
turns.zh: 这是一个非常好的观点，我没有想到要问这个。但在这种情况下，这是一家公司内的初创公司做得很好，我也同意，它很少起作用，但在这里却做到了。您认为让它发挥作用的关键是什么？我知道你刚才谈到了这个问题，你会如何总结，“这是每个人在一家新的大公司里开始做一些小事情时应该做的事情”？

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: There are some macro things where, I do believe we were children of fortune, like mobile, et cetera. When I joined Cash App a lot of the people working on it were fairly tenured, both at Square and just like in their careers, and had done sort of really meaningful things. And as a consequence, I do think there's like... This is a thing I haven't quite been able to articulate well, but there was something around a small, tightly-knit senior team super focused on a problem. And the smallness means just like, less prior miscommunication, and then the tightly-knit means a lot more trust. And then I think Brian was obviously just, he'd been at Square for a long time, he knew the organization well, was a color operator on there, knew like talent, like who was good that he wanted to bring on board. (17:52): And I think that combination of things... Well, not my guess is, there are other things. But I think without that thing, it would actually have been really, really difficult.
turns.zh: 在一些宏观事物上，我确实相信我们是财富之子，比如移动设备等等。当我加入 Cash App 时，很多从事该项目的人都获得了相当的终身职位，无论是在 Square 还是在他们的职业生涯中，都做了一些真正有意义的事情。因此，我确实认为……这是我无法很好地表达的事情，但是围绕着一个小型的、紧密结合的高级团队，他们超级专注于一个问题。规模小意味着之前的沟通不畅会减少，而紧密的联系意味着更多的信任。然后我认为布莱恩显然是公正的，他在 Square 工作了很长时间，他很了解这个组织，是那里的色彩操作员，知道人才，知道他想引进谁是优秀的。 (17:52)：我认为这些事情的结合......嗯，不是我的猜测，还有其他事情。但我认为如果没有那个东西，这实际上会非常非常困难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's an awesome lesson, just like a small, trusted team that has seniority, and leadership trusts to operate and not just like, "Hey, what the hell are you doing? It's time to share faster."
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个很棒的教训，就像一个值得信赖的小团队，有资历，领导层信任他们的运作，而​​不仅仅是“嘿，你到底在做什么？是时候更快地分享了。”

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: The Cash App team stayed super senior for a long time.
turns.zh: Cash App 团队长期担任高级职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. And you said small, how small would you... Was it/what do you recommend when you say it should be a small team for something like this?
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。你说小，你会多小......当你说应该是一个小团队来做这样的事情时，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: You know, a lot depends on the thing, I don't think there's a one-shot answer. When I joined Cash App it was like 11 or 12, and it wasn't much more than that for like a year. And I forget how big it was when I left, but we had real scale in a real business before we had a real head count, I guess is the way I would say it.
turns.zh: 你知道，这很大程度上取决于具体情况，我不认为有一个一次性的答案。当我加入 Cash App 的时候，大概有 11 或 12 个，而且一年之内也没有多多少。我忘记了我离开时它有多大，但在我们拥有真正的员工人数之前，我们在真正的业务中已经有了真正的规模，我想这就是我所说的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it, yeah.
turns.zh: 喜欢它，是的。

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: And you kind of had to fight for every head count. And I think the head count at this point was a Sarah Fryer thing from Square, she was just really, really disciplined about making sure that if you were trying to bring people on and spend the company's money, you really just fight it.
turns.zh: 而且你必须为每一个人而战。我认为此时的员工数量是来自 Square 的 Sarah Fryer 的作品，她非常非常自律，确保如果你试图吸引员工并花公司的钱，你真的会反抗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a really good takeaway. Let's transition to talking about what you're currently doing, Carbon Health. You went from consumer fin tech to consumer health tech, first of all just real quick, just how did that transition happen? Was that something you planned, or is that just like you went on exploring and that's where you ended up?
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个非常好的外卖。让我们转向谈论您目前正在做的事情，碳健康。您从消费者金融科技转向消费者健康科技，首先速度非常快，这种转变是如何发生的？这是你计划好的事情，还是就像你不断探索并最终到达的地方？

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: It was more I went on exploring, that's where I ended up. I'd say there was maybe three parts, there's one part where when I was exploring there was this guy, Russell Fradin, who now works at Carbon, who had... He introduced me to like a third of my network in Silicon Valley. And basically he said, "Hey, there's this guy who's amazing, he was the founder of Udemy, and now he started this company called Carbon Health. His name's Eren, you need to talk to him." And I was like, "Sure." And Eren, I met, and Eren is brilliant, and also had this crazy way of explaining a complex problem in a way that made the solution obvious. And so he was like, "Oh yeah," like, "Here's how we're going to do it, and here's the thing we spent two and a half hours together." (20:17): And then at the end I was like, "Oh yeah, this is obvious, somebody should just build this thing." And then I think the second part was, I think everyone's the hero in their own story, I'm no different. So I think when I left Cash App, and when I was thinking about [inaudible 00:20:33] I was thinking of starting a company and doing all this stuff. And one of the muscles that we really just spent a lot of time building Cash App was going really, really deep into like the regulatory sort of wallpaper of the problems we were trying to solve. And so we would have sessions where we'd be sitting in a room, like product, engineering, legal, compliance, et cetera, with some regs literally blown up on a projector screen, and a section of text highlighted, and being like, "Hey, what does this really mean? (21:02): "Okay, what if we build a product this way? What if we structure money movement this way," et cetera. And so I casted myself instead as, "Hey, what if I could be good at regulated businesses, instead of just good at money?" And that was the way that I tied the two together. There were a bunch of other sort of very personal ego things, like, "I want to build a team that's mostly founders." Both my parents were doctors, and I'd been through some sort of scary experiences in the healthcare system. So there was just like a part of it that was about sort of mission and background, but the career part was really about, how do you stick the two things together? And I also wanted to learn... There was this thing that happened in my like fourth year at Cash App where I was like, "Oh, there's this other thing that we have to build that would be amazing if we actually built it." (21:54): Which is what Pinwheel, the company I'm on the board of, actually is. So I was like, "Hey, we've got to build this platform for payroll," it's like the last giant money movement thing that hasn't really come to move the needle in a long time. And I couldn't get the organization convinced to build it, which kind of is what it is, A. And B, I was like, "Oh, I want to have that insight. Can I have that insight of like what the second thing is faster the same time around?" And I am sad to report that three years in Carbon, I have not had it yet.
turns.zh: 我更多的是继续探索，这就是我的结局。我想说可能有三个部分，其中一个部分是，当我探索时，有一个人，Russell Fradin，他现在在 Carbon 工作，他……他向我介绍了我在硅谷的三分之一的人际网络。基本上他说，“嘿，这个人很了不起，他是 Udemy 的创始人，现在他创办了这家名为 Carbon Health 的公司。他的名字叫 Eren，你需要和他谈谈。”我说：“当然。”我遇到了艾伦，他很聪明，而且还用这种疯狂的方式解释了一个复杂的问题，使解决方案变得显而易见。所以他说，“哦，是的，”就像，“这就是我们要做的事情，这就是我们一起度过了两个半小时的事情。” (20:17)：最后我想，“哦，是的，这很明显，有人应该建造这个东西。”然后我认为第二部分是，我认为每个人都是自己故事中的英雄，我也不例外。所以我想当我离开 Cash App 时，当我考虑 [听不清 00:20:33] 时，我正在考虑创办一家公司并做所有这些事情。我们花了很多时间构建 Cash App 的一大优势是非常非常深入地研究我们试图解决的问题的监管壁纸。所以我们会坐在一个房间里举行会议，比如产品、工程、法律、合规等等，一些法规在投影仪屏幕上放大，一段文本突出显示，然后说，“嘿，这到底是什么意思？（21:02）：“好吧，如果我们用这种方式构建一个产品怎么办？如果我们以这种方式构建货币流动，会怎样？”等等。所以我把自己定位为：“嘿，如果我能擅长受监管的业务，而不仅仅是擅长赚钱呢？”这就是我将两者联系在一起的方式。还有很多其他非常个人的自我意识，比如，“我想建立一个主要由创始人组成的团队。”我的父母都是医生，我在医疗保健系统中经历过一些可怕的经历。所以就像其中一部分是关于使命和背景，但职业部分实际上是关于如何将这两件事结合在一起？我也想学习......在我在 Cash App 的第四年发生了一件事情，我当时想，“哦，如果我们真的建造它，那将是令人惊奇的。”（21:54）：这就是我所加入的公司 Pinwheel 的实际情况，所以我当时想，“嘿，我们必须建立这个薪资平台，”这就像最后一次巨大的资金流动，但很长一段时间以来都没有真正发挥作用。我无法说服组织建立它，这就是它的本质，A。而B，我当时想，“哦，我想有这种洞察力。我能洞察到第二件事同时更快吗？”我很遗憾地告诉大家，在 Carbon 工作了三年，我还没有体会到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've got a lot going on, I am not surprised. So I was going to ask, what draws you towards highly-regulated industries being at Cash App? And I like that you already went there, basically you just found that that's maybe the thing that you could get really smart at, and that applies to a lot of different markets. That's an interesting insight about yourself, like, "This could be the thing that I get good at."
turns.zh: 你发生了很多事情，我并不感到惊讶。所以我想问，是什么吸引您在 Cash App 中选择高度监管的行业？我喜欢你已经去过那里，基本上你只是发现这可能是你可以真正聪明的事情，并且适用于很多不同的市场。这是对你自己的一个有趣的洞察，比如，“这可能是我擅长的事情。”

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, or differentially better at than other people.
turns.zh: 是的，是的，或者比其他人更擅长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You kind of like mentioned this off to the side, this idea that you like to hire founders. And can you speak more to that, just like what that means in your day-to-day, and then maybe how your team looks today. Is it mostly founders, or some [inaudible 00:23:05]?
turns.zh: 你有点像顺便提到了这一点，即你喜欢聘请创始人。您能否详细谈谈这一点，就像这在您的日常生活中意味着什么，然后也许您的团队今天的样子。主要是创始人，还是一些[听不清 00:23:05]？

turns.speaker: Ayo Omojola
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I think the team looks today about half and half. So I had this experience going through IC, where... And just kind of growing up, my career in Silicon Valley, where I knew a bunch of founders who were absolute beasts, like incredible people, could do amazing things, and they would bounce off organizations. They would be like, "All right, I'm going to go work at Amazon," and just not last. And when I was at Cash App I went through a bunch of hiring processes where I was like, "Hey, we should try and hire some founders to do this, look at these companies," et cetera. And a thing that would happen that... And this part really isn't about founders, although founders are like one way sort of this happens. (23:49): But a thing that would happen quite often is, by the time that as a hiring manager you get a bunch of resumes to look at, like you post the job, a bunch of people apply, you're partnering with a sourcer, by the time you get a bunch of resumes to look at they've screened out everyone that doesn't just like fit inside a box. And it's like, at Google, Facebook, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, and then at certain set of schools, and then a certain type of experience, et cetera. (33:26): Is there new tech we can take advantage of, will the people even talk to us? Is the thing we're talking about even possible? And we ended up doing... At the time there was a... (34:09): And this is like, again, a thing that I learned, which we went through. And then a lot of the stuff we did around our regulatory work, around prepaid, building a digital wallet, et cetera, made me realize that like a thing that would happen very frequently is, you want to work on something and you go talk to an expert. And usually for most people, an expert is not like, hey, the most expert person in the world, because that's a very, very hard thing to know who that is, especially when you're not an expert. (35:08): Usually an expert is the most tenured person in the world in the domain that you're questioning, and the length of tenure, and the depth of experience actually can vary very wildly from person to person. (35:55): So the way that I apply that today, and I'm sure people at Carbon will tell you this, is I end up asking lots of questions that people think don't matter, because I'm like, "Hey, we're trying to optimize something." turns.zh: 这是我从 Cash App 中摘下来的，当时...当我们开发 Cash Card 时，第一个...就像 2015 年、2016 年，Cash Card 的第一次迭代，Cash App 的设计主管 Robert Anderson，这个人是一位了不起的设计师，如果可以的话请雇用他，他喜欢这个设计。他说，“嘿，我有这个设计，我们要做这个事情。”我说：“太棒了。”也许我会得到一些草图文件？ PDF、pre-figma。我们将它们邮寄给一些卡供应商，他们寄回给我们的东西就像是，你会把它作为你生活中、世界上的产品吗？比如，你在做什么？结果，布莱恩说，“嘿，我们只是需要有人来弄清楚如何制作这个东西。”所以我最终花了很长时间去全国各地不同的卡片制造工厂，弄清楚卡片是如何制作的，有哪些可能性？ (33:26)：我们可以利用新技术吗？人们会和我们交谈吗？我们正在谈论的事情有可能吗？我们最终做了...当时有一个...我不会说超级新，它已经在[听不清00:33:38]上出现了几年，但它还没有出现在主流卡上，这种激光雕刻的概念。事实证明，用于制作激光雕刻卡片的机器具有数千种设置组合，所有这些组合都会产生不同的物理效果。就像你可以增加功率设置并真正燃烧塑料一样，你会得到一种红色、粗糙的纹理。你可以降低功率设置，减小光圈，你会得到非常精细、平滑的一致性。 (34:09)：这又像是我学到的、我们经历过的事情。在塑料、覆盖层、纸张、信封和饰面之间，很容易就有 1,000 种组合，然后我们才喜欢上发货的第一个版本的现金卡。还有一个团队仍然在那里，仍然在做真正的物理卡片对象，与市场上存在的任何东西都不一样，就像进入差异化领域一样。然后我们围绕监管工作、预付费、构建数字钱包等所做的很多事情让我意识到，就像经常发生的事情一样，你想要做某件事，然后去与专家交谈。通常对于大多数人来说，专家并不像，嘿，世界上最专家的人，因为要知道他是谁是一件非常非常困难的事情，尤其是当你不是专家时。 (35:08)：通常专家是您所质疑的领域中世界上任期最长的人，任期的长短和经验的深度实际上因人而异。所以发生的事情就像，你去问某人一些事情，他们会给你一个答案，就像他们认为是真的一样，他们没有撒谎，也没有恶意，这只是他妈的书呆子。你只需要继续努力，直到得到答案，就像我真的不知道如何正确地表达这个问题一样。但这有点像，不到达终点就不能停下来。这就是为什么处于重要领域非常重要的原因之一，因为如果您处于小型团队环境中，这是一项非常非常昂贵的活动。 (35:55)：所以我今天应用的方式，我相信 Carbon 的人会告诉你这一点，是我最终问了很多人们认为不重要的问题，因为我想，“嘿，我们正在尝试优化一些东西。”通常我发现，当你第一次尝试优化某些东西时，他们并没有针对它进行优化。你实际上必须重新测量它，你必须重新检测它，你必须从头开始重建所有查询、所有视觉效果等等。你必须用 15 种不同的方式来看待它们，然后每当有两件事不一致时，你就必须去找出原因，这就像一项乏味的工作。在受监管的行业中，我认为这是......（36:38）：我的猜测是，在几乎任何具有很多变量的复杂环境中，这最终都会成为现实，这有点......而且它们越受限制[听不清00:36:48]，我认为实际上这更重要，你无法避免细节，你只需要深入了解它们。如果你不这样做，你仍然可以做得很好，但这实际上更可能是运气而不是技能。
